title: Columbus Inventory Up 7%: What a Quieter Summer Market Means
author: CRE News Newsroom
excerpt: The Columbus housing market saw inventory climb 7% in August, reaching 2.2 months of supply. Prices are holding above $335K, and sellers still command 98.5% of asking price.
body:
Central Ohio's housing inventory climbed roughly 7% year-over-year in August 2026, pushing local supply to about 2.2 months — the most slack buyers have seen since early 2020. Prices haven't buckled: the regional median is above $335,000, with homes still closing near 98.5% of asking price.

## The Numbers Behind the Shift

The Columbus REALTORS® June 2026 report — the most recent full data set from the trade association — counted 1,563 closed sales in central Ohio, a 7.8% jump from the same month a year earlier. The median sale price in Franklin County reached $352,000 in June, up just 0.6% from June 2025.

Those two figures tell a quietly important story: volume went up, but appreciation slowed. More buyers closed deals, but sellers didn't need to discount sharply to make that happen.

At the individual listing level, the shift shows up in days on market. The average central Ohio home is now spending roughly 47 days under contract, according to a Wayne Woods market analysis tracking August conditions — a meaningful stretch from the pandemic-era pace, when well-located properties regularly drew multiple offers within 48 to 72 hours. Redfin's Columbus data, using a three-month rolling window through July, puts the figure at 39 days. The difference reflects geographic scope (Columbus proper versus the broader metro) and measurement windows, not a factual contradiction. Both figures point the same direction: buyers have time to think.

## What 2.2 Months of Supply Actually Means

Real estate practitioners traditionally describe a balanced market as four to six months of housing supply — roughly the time it would take to sell every active listing at the current sales pace with no new inventory added. At 2.2 months, Columbus is still firmly in seller's market territory.

The distinction matters: a more balanced market is not the same as a fully balanced one. Sellers in desirable Columbus neighborhoods — Upper Arlington, Grandview, Powell, and the Clintonville corridor — are not under pressure. Properties that are well-priced, recently updated, and marketed correctly are still selling near full asking price. The 98.5% sale-to-list ratio confirms that discipline: a $335,000 listing is clearing at roughly $329,775 on average. That is not a discount market.

What has changed is the cost of getting the price wrong. Overpricing above comparable sales — a strategy that sometimes worked when multiple-offer dynamics covered the gap — is now a much riskier move. Buyers have alternatives. Listings that sit on the market too long attract questions about condition and motivation that become harder to answer over time.

## How Columbus Compares to the National Picture

Columbus is bucking a national trend in a meaningful way. The National Association of Realtors reported that existing-home sales fell 1.7% in July 2026 to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.06 million — the lowest reading in more than a year — as the 30-year fixed mortgage rate reached its 2026 high. The national median sale price hit $434,100, a new record.

Columbus's June closed sales rising 7.8% while the national figure declined speaks to the local market's relative affordability. Franklin County's $352,000 median is roughly 19% below the national median, and the region's economy — still buoyed by Intel's New Albany semiconductor campus construction and steady in-migration from costlier metros — is generating buyer demand that national softness has not yet erased.

Zillow's July 2026 national market report flagged leading indicators pointing toward a slower second half of the year. In Columbus, that deceleration is arriving more gently, from a stronger base.

## What Buyers Should Know

The most practical fact for buyers today is that the decision window is no longer measured in hours. Scheduling a showing, completing a home inspection, and comparing two or three listings before writing an offer is once again a reasonable strategy in most Columbus neighborhoods.

Calendar flexibility is not the same as pricing leverage, though. In a market with a 98.5% sale-to-list ratio and 2.2 months of supply, aggressive lowball offers are still likely to fail in competitive corridors. The more useful buyer strategy is precision: knowing which submarkets have softened (often suburban attached housing and townhomes) versus which remain tight (close-in single-family in walkable, well-regarded school districts).

Buyers often have better luck targeting inspection credits for deferred maintenance or negotiating closing cost assistance — concessions sellers are more likely to grant than headline price reductions.

## What Sellers Should Know

Sellers entering the late-summer and fall Columbus market face a smaller pool of active buyers than the spring peak, but demand has not evaporated. The 7.8% year-over-year increase in June closed sales shows the Columbus buyer base is healthy.

The strategic risk has shifted from whether a home will sell to whether it will sell at the price the seller needs. Sellers who price accurately and present the home well remain in a strong position. Those who anchor to an outdated comparable and refuse to adjust will find themselves sitting — and a listing that lingers in Columbus's late-summer market invites skepticism about what the seller isn't disclosing.

For landlords and investors in the Short North, [Franklinton](/areas/franklinton), and Near East corridors, rents have remained relatively firm through mid-year even as the for-sale market rebalances.

## The Bottom Line

Columbus's summer housing market is not a crash, a correction, or a buyer's bonanza. It is a rebalancing — the gradual restoration of negotiating friction after a period when sellers held near-total pricing power and buyers had almost none.

For anyone making a housing decision this fall, the question is less about whether the market is good or bad and more about which neighborhoods, price bands, and property types are actually shifting. The answer is hyperlocal, not regional. And in Columbus right now, the regional headline is that things are — carefully, cautiously — getting more normal.
